overview.summary: Data engineers build and maintain the systems that collect, store and move data so that analysts and data scientists can use it.
overview.problems: They make sure data is accurate, organized and available when people need it, even when it comes from many sources.
overview.worksWith: Data scientists, analysts, software engineers, business teams and cloud or security engineers.
overview.workplaces: Technology companies, banks, retailers, hospitals and other organizations that use data, often in offices or remotely.

timeline.title: Check data pipelines
timeline.description: The engineer looks for overnight failures or delays in data flows.
timeline.why: Many reports depend on data arriving on time.

timeline.title: Building pipelines
timeline.description: The engineer writes code that collects data from different sources, cleans it and loads it into storage.
timeline.why: Reliable pipelines are the base of analytics.

timeline.title: Fixing data problems
timeline.description: The engineer finds out why numbers do not match, such as missing values or duplicate records.
timeline.why: Wrong data leads to wrong decisions.

timeline.title: Working with analysts
timeline.description: The engineer learns what data analysts need and shapes it for them.
timeline.why: Data is only useful if people can use it.

timeline.title: Documentation and testing
timeline.description: The engineer writes tests and notes so others can trust and maintain the work.
timeline.why: Tested, documented systems break less often.

timeline.title: On-call and incidents
timeline.description: When a pipeline breaks, the team restores it, sometimes out of hours.
timeline.why: Business decisions may depend on the data being fresh.

responsibilities: Designing storage systems such as databases and warehouses
Making data secure and following privacy rules
challenges: Data from different sources is often messy and inconsistent.
Pipeline failures can affect many reports and need quick repair.
The work is often invisible until something breaks.
Privacy and security rules need careful handling.
Strong programming and database skills are usually needed before entry.
workEnvironment: Mostly desk and computer based, in offices or remotely, working with analysts and developers. Hours are often regular but data problems can bring urgent work.
rewards: Building the base that data work depends on
Strong demand for data skills in many sectors
A mix of coding and design
tradeoffs: Titles and pay that vary by country and employer

activity.title: Clean a messy table
steps: In a spreadsheet, type a small made-up table of ten students with names, ages and favourite subjects, with mistakes such as different spellings of the same subject, a missing age and a duplicate row.
Find and fix each problem, making the format consistent.
Write a short list of the rules you used.
Count how many problems you found.
Note whether tidying data felt satisfying.
activity.outcome: You practise spotting and fixing data quality problems and writing rules.
activity.safety: Use only made-up data, never real names or personal details of other people, and do not upload data to any website without an adult.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
